item.text:
**Initial Evidence Note: Sheikh Hasina in 2024**

Scope: I selected only a small set of high-credibility web sources and kept 2024 events separate from background context. Question IDs below are **inferred** from generic ruler-quality themes because I did not use the repository rubric in this isolated workflow.

**2024 Events**
- **Claim:** Hasina’s January 2024 election returned her to office for a fourth consecutive term, but the vote was widely criticized as boycotted, violent, and low-turnout.
  - **Source:** [Hasina wins Bangladesh vote, but low turnout and opposition boycott raise doubts over its legitimacy](https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/ap-top-news/2024/01/06/fear-of-violence-looms-over-a-contentious-bangladesh-election-as-polls-open/) — Associated Press, **January 6-7, 2024**
  - **Summary:** AP reported Hasina’s Awami League won a strong majority while the main opposition boycotted the vote; turnout was about 40%, and legitimacy doubts were widespread.
  - **QIDs informed:** 7A.* (legitimacy / political competition), 8B.* (governance / control), 8A.* (stability)

- **Claim:** The United States and United Kingdom publicly said the January election extending Hasina’s rule was not credible, free, or fair.
  - **Source:** [The US and UK say Bangladesh's elections extending Hasina's rule were not credible](https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/ap-top-news/2024/01/09/the-us-and-uk-say-bangladeshs-elections-extending-hasinas-rule-were-not-credible) — Associated Press, **January 8, 2024**
  - **Summary:** This is strong external confirmation that the 2024 election was viewed negatively by key foreign partners.
  - **QIDs informed:** 7A.* (electoral legitimacy), 7B.* (political openness), 8B.*

- **Claim:** Bangladesh’s economy showed a strong post-COVID turnaround in early 2024, but inflation, external balance stress, and financial-sector weakness remained serious problems.
  - **Source:** [Financial Sector and Fiscal Policy Reforms Will Help Bangladesh Sustain Strong Growth](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/04/02/financial-sector-and-fiscal-policy-reforms-will-help-bangladesh-sustain-strong-growth-despite-strong-growth-south-asia-r) — World Bank, **April 2, 2024**
  - **Summary:** Favorable on growth momentum, but clearly mixed: high inflation eroded purchasing power, reserves were under pressure, and reforms were needed.
  - **QIDs informed:** 8B.* (policy/economic performance), 6A.* (economic management), 6B.*

- **Claim:** Bangladesh had a long-run development record that remained materially positive by early 2024.
  - **Source:** [The World Bank In Bangladesh 2024](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099514001022413953) — World Bank, **December 31, 2023 / disclosed January 2, 2024**
  - **Summary:** World Bank described “remarkable development progress,” including lower-middle-income status, gender parity in school enrollment, and major mortality reductions.
  - **QIDs informed:** 6A.* (development outcomes), 8B.* (state capacity), 4A.* (social performance)

- **Claim:** By late July 2024, the government response to student protests had escalated into a severe crackdown with internet shutdowns, curfews, army deployment, and large-scale casualties.
  - **Source:** [Bangladesh: Türk decries government crackdown, urges respect for international human rights standards](https://bangladesh.un.org/en/275065-bangladesh-t%C3%BCrk-decries-government-crackdown-urges-respect-international-human-rights) — United Nations / OHCHR, **July 26, 2024**
  - **Summary:** The UN human-rights chief said more than 170 people had been killed, condemned the crackdown, and warned that internet shutdowns reduce scrutiny and increase impunity.
  - **QIDs informed:** 7C.* (repression / rights violations), 8A.* (crisis handling), 8B.*

- **Claim:** Reuters reported that Bangladesh had imposed communications restrictions and a curfew while soldiers patrolled Dhaka during the July protests.
  - **Source:** [Bangladesh army enforces curfew as student-led protests spiral](https://theprint.in/world/bangladesh-army-enforces-curfew-as-student-led-protests-spiral/2182818/) — Reuters, **July 20, 2024**
  - **Summary:** Reuters described the country being cut off from internet/text services and under curfew after deadly protest violence, reinforcing the severity of the crisis.
  - **QIDs informed:** 7C.* (coercion / repression), 8A.* (order maintenance), 8B.*

- **Claim:** Hasina resigned and fled Bangladesh on August 5, 2024 after the protest crisis overwhelmed her government.
  - **Source:** [Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina resigns, interim government to be formed](https://theprint.in/world/bangladesh-pm-sheikh-hasina-resigns-interim-government-to-be-formed/2208572/) — Reuters, **August 5, 2024**
  - **Summary:** Reuters reported that she left the country and that an interim government would be formed, marking the collapse of her rule in 2024.
  - **QIDs informed:** 8A.* (regime continuity / control), 8B.* (crisis outcome), 7A.*

- **Claim:** In September 2024, the UN opened a fact-finding process into human-rights violations tied to the July-August protests.
  - **Source:** [UN Fact-Finding Team Issues Call for Submissions](https://bangladesh.un.org/en/278741-un-fact-finding-team-issues-call-submissions) — United Nations in Bangladesh / OHCHR, **September 16, 2024**
  - **Summary:** The UN said it was investigating alleged violations between July 1 and August 15, 2024, which is strong corroboration that the year’s events were serious and well documented.
  - **QIDs informed:** 7C.* (rights / accountability), 8A.*, 8B.*

**Bottom Line**
- The 2024 term looked **highly unstable and increasingly repressive**, especially from July onward.
- The year begins with a **contested election and low legitimacy**, then shifts into **mass protest, state coercion, communications shutdowns, and regime collapse**.
- The main favorable evidence is **structural, not political**: Bangladesh still had real development gains and some macroeconomic resilience, but those positives were outweighed in 2024 by the legitimacy and rights crisis.
